![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/9e7c8d7f80211aebbd8a8fb5456e2bfe0a5dd0dc46addfe65777eb09f0b4c66a.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of a continuous function $y=f(x)$, is given above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point:  

$\,$ $x=3$  

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical point. Consider the vertical lines $x=3$ and choose an arbitrary point on it.

So, we draw it as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/4aa4592a6edae5207c7e934aa148e87dd8a8762f6bbdba260cc137bd64b407b9.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(2,3)$ and decreasing $↘$ on $(3,\infty )$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=3.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is a positive constant to the left of $x=2$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ represents a section of an increasing  straight line on $(-\infty ,2).$ Also, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is decreasing to the right of $x=2$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)<0.$ So, the curve $y=f(x)$ is concave down on $(2,\infty ).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/347dda820c8307984b88ffb5f2b528c20984ec8a7e9acbe9b7f3d8f457a917b2.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/99de5224b614ea11b454020d7a165b58ff0fcf47708faba9973255276133eebc.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
